title: Claude Agent Teams Over Pilot
description: Connect Claude-powered agents into teams using Pilot Protocol. Encrypted P2P communication for Anthropic agent workflows.
seoTitle: Claude Agent Teams Over Pilot | Pilot Protocol Blog
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: Code introduced agent teams: a manager agent that delegates work to specialist agents, each operating in its own context window and git worktree. The architecture is powerful. The manager breaks a complex task into subtasks, assigns them to specialists (frontend, backend, testing, infrastructure), and synthesizes the results. Each specialist gets a full 200K context window, isolated file access, and focused instructions.

There is one constraint: all agents run on the same machine. The manager and every specialist share a single computer's CPU, memory, and disk. What if your backend specialist needs a GPU server? What if your QA specialist should run in the CI environment? What if your infrastructure specialist needs access to cloud credentials that should never leave the production VPN? This article shows how Pilot Protocol removes the single-machine constraint and distributes Claude agent teams across machines, networks, and even organizations.
How Claude Code Agent Teams Work Today
Before we distribute them, let us understand the current model. When you use Claude Code's agent team feature, here is what happens:
It receives the high-level task ("build a user authentication system") and plans the subtasks.
The manager creates specialist agents with focused roles: "frontend-auth" gets the React components, "backend-auth" gets the API routes, "test-auth" gets the test files.
Each specialist operates in its own git worktree, so file edits do not conflict. The manager can merge results after each specialist completes.
Each specialist gets its own 200K token context window. The manager's context is not consumed by specialist work.
Specialists return their results (files modified, tests written, commands run) to the manager, which synthesizes them into the final output.

This is effective for parallelizing work across multiple Claude instances. But the execution is local. Every specialist is a subprocess on the same machine, accessing the same filesystem (via worktrees), using the same network, limited to the same hardware.

A manager on a MacBook Pro spawns 4 specialists. Each specialist drives a Claude API session that produces code. But the ML specialist cannot train a model because there is no GPU. The load testing specialist cannot run a realistic benchmark because it would saturate the MacBook's network. The infrastructure specialist has no access to the staging environment's AWS credentials. Same-machine execution works for code generation. It breaks for anything that needs specialized hardware, network position, or credentials.

The core idea: replace the local subprocess model with Pilot Protocol's encrypted messaging. Instead of spawning a specialist as a subprocess, the manager sends work to a specialist running on a different machine. The specialist receives the message, executes the work (using its own Claude API key, its own hardware, its own network position), and returns the results over an encrypted Pilot tunnel.
Each machine in the distributed team runs:
- handles peer discovery, tunnel encryption, NAT traversal
- accepts tasks matching its specialty, executes them with Claude, returns results
The manager machine runs the manager agent, which has

available as a tool. When the manager decides to delegate work, it sends a message to the specialist over an encrypted Pilot tunnel. The Pilot network handles everything else: finding the specialist, establishing the encrypted connection, and transferring the work payload and results.

as a tool. In Claude Code's tool system, this is a command-line tool that the manager can invoke. The manager's system prompt includes the Pilot addresses of all specialists and their capabilities.

fields.code:
# Manager's tool: send a task to a specialist and wait for its reply
pilotctl --json send-message 0:0000.0004.1A02 --wait 15m --data \
  '{"description":"Implement user authentication API routes","params":{"framework":"gin","endpoints":"login,logout,register,refresh","auth_method":"jwt"}}'
# the specialist's reply comes back inline under data.reply

# Replies that arrive after the wait are kept in the inbox
pilotctl --json inbox --from 0:0000.0004.1A02 --latest

You have access to the following specialist agents via Pilot Protocol:

Backend specialist (0:0000.0004.1A02):
  - Go and Python backend development
  - API design, database schemas, server configuration
  - Has access to staging database credentials

ML specialist (0:0000.0004.1A03):

QA specialist (0:0000.0004.1A04):
  - Test writing, load testing, benchmarking
  - Runs in CI environment with access to test databases
  - Can execute full test suites and report coverage

To delegate work, use:

Trust is already established between all agents.

children.text: Each specialist machine runs a worker agent that polls its inbox for tasks, executes them with the
, and returns results. Here is a Python implementation:

fields.code:
import subprocess
import json
import anthropic
import sys
import time

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

SPECIALTY = sys.argv[1]  # "backend", "ml", or "qa"

SYSTEM_PROMPTS = {
    "backend": """You are a backend development specialist.
You write production-quality Go and Python code.
You have access to the local filesystem and can create/modify files.
Return your work as a list of files created or modified.""",

    "ml": """You are a machine learning specialist.
You have access to a GPU (A100) and standard ML libraries.
You can train models, run evaluations, and produce reports.
Return results as files and summary text.""",

    "qa": """You are a QA specialist.
You write and execute tests. You run benchmarks.
You have access to test databases and CI tooling.
Return test results, coverage reports, and any failing test details.""",
}

handled = set()  # inbox message IDs already processed

def new_tasks():
    """Inbox messages not handled yet, oldest first."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["pilotctl", "--json", "inbox", "--limit", "0", "--full"],
        capture_output=True, text=True
    )
    if out.returncode != 0:
        return []
    messages = json.loads(out.stdout)["data"]["messages"]  # newest first
    return [m for m in reversed(messages) if m["id"] not in handled]

def recv_and_execute():
    while True:
        tasks = new_tasks()
        if not tasks:
            time.sleep(2)
            continue

        for msg in tasks:
            handled.add(msg["id"])
            run_task(msg)

def run_task(msg):
    sender = msg.get("from", "unknown")
    task = json.loads(msg.get("data") or "{}")
    print(f"Received task from {sender}: {task.get('description', '')}")

    # Build the prompt from task description and params
    prompt = f"Task: {task.get('description', '')}\n\n"
    params = task.get("params", {})
    if params:
        prompt += "Parameters:\n"
        for k, v in params.items():
            prompt += f"  {k}: {v}\n"

    # Execute with Claude API
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
        max_tokens=8192,
        system=SYSTEM_PROMPTS[SPECIALTY],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )

    result_text = response.content[0].text
    print(f"Task completed, sending results back to {sender}...")

    # Return results via pilotctl (lands in the manager's inbox)
    subprocess.run(["pilotctl", "send-message", sender, "--data", result_text])
    print(f"Results sent to {sender}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"Worker started: specialty={SPECIALTY}")
    recv_and_execute()

Security in a distributed agent team has different requirements than a public marketplace. Here is how to configure trust for a private team:
The manager must be able to submit tasks to every specialist. On the manager machine:

fields.code:
# Manager trusts each specialist
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0004.1A02  # backend
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0004.1A03  # ml
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0004.1A04  # qa

children.text: Specialists should only accept tasks from the authorized manager. On each specialist machine:

fields.code:
# Specialist trusts only the manager
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0004.1A01  # manager

children.text: This creates a hub-and-spoke trust topology. The manager can reach all specialists. Each specialist can only be reached by the manager. Specialists cannot submit tasks to each other unless explicitly granted trust. This prevents a compromised specialist from using other specialists as an attack surface.
For teams where specialists need peer communication (e.g., the backend specialist sends test fixtures to the QA specialist), add explicit trust between those specific pairs:

fields.code:
# On the QA specialist: also trust the backend specialist
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0004.1A02  # backend can send to qa
# On the backend specialist: the matching handshake (or pilotctl approve)
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0004.1A04

children.text: Trust is not transitive. Trusting the manager does not mean trusting the manager's other specialists. Every trust relationship is an explicit, mutual Ed25519 handshake. See
File Transfer Between Manager and Specialists
Claude agent teams work heavily with files. The manager needs to send source files to specialists and receive modified files back. Pilot's data exchange service (port 1001) handles this:

fields.code:
# Manager sends source files to the backend specialist (send-file takes one file)
tar czf auth-src.tgz ./src/auth/
pilotctl send-file 0:0000.0004.1A02 auth-src.tgz

# Backend specialist sends modified files back
tar czf auth-out.tgz ./output/auth/
pilotctl send-file 0:0000.0004.1A01 auth-out.tgz

The file transfer is encrypted through the same tunnel as everything else. No separate file server, no S3 bucket, no shared filesystem. Direct agent-to-agent transfer over the encrypted overlay.

Complex agent teams need more than request-response. Every daemon runs an event stream broker (port 1002) for publish-subscribe. Publishers and subscribers target a peer's broker, so pick one team member's daemon as the shared broker, here the ML specialist's (
), and have the others publish and subscribe there. Topics match exactly; the only wildcard is

fields.code:
# Manager subscribes to every topic on the shared broker
pilotctl subscribe 0:0000.0004.1A03 "*"

# Backend specialist publishes when API is ready
pilotctl publish 0:0000.0004.1A03 specialist.backend.ready \
  --data '{"endpoints": ["POST /auth/login", "POST /auth/register"]}'

# QA specialist subscribes to that exact topic
# (and starts testing when the backend is ready)
pilotctl subscribe 0:0000.0004.1A03 specialist.backend.ready

children.text: This enables reactive workflows. The QA specialist does not need to poll for task completion. It subscribes to "specialist.backend.ready" and begins testing when the backend code is available. The manager subscribes to "*" and gets a real-time view of all specialist activity. Events are delivered at most once to subscribers connected at that moment; there is no replay. See
Distributed Claude agent teams over Pilot Protocol open up scenarios that are impossible with same-machine execution:

Company A has a frontend team with Claude agents that produce React components. Company B has a backend team with Claude agents that build APIs. Their agents use the same registry, with mutual trust between the integration specialist agents. Company A's manager submits "build API for user dashboard" to Company B's backend specialist. The result flows back over an encrypted tunnel. Neither company's internal code leaves their network; only the task description and results cross the boundary.

An ML team has three GPU servers and five CPU-only development machines. GPU agents specialize in training and inference tasks. CPU agents handle code generation, testing, and documentation. The manager routes tasks based on hardware requirements: model fine-tuning goes to GPU agents, API development goes to CPU agents.

A global team runs specialists in different regions for latency-sensitive testing. The US specialist tests against US-region databases. The EU specialist tests against EU-region databases for GDPR compliance verification. The APAC specialist tests against APAC endpoints for latency benchmarks. The manager delegates region-specific QA tasks to the appropriate specialist. Pilot's

CI/CD pipelines spawn specialist agents as needed. A GitHub Actions workflow starts a Pilot daemon, registers the CI runner as a QA specialist, receives a test task from the manager, executes it, returns results, and shuts down. The next pipeline run creates a fresh specialist with a fresh environment.
Let us walk through a complete scenario. The manager receives: "Add two-factor authentication to the user login flow."

fields.code:
# Step 1: Manager analyzes and decomposes the task
# (This happens in the manager's Claude context)
# Subtasks: backend API, frontend UI, tests, documentation

# Step 2: Manager sends backend task
pilotctl --json send-message 0:0000.0004.1A02 --wait 15m --data \
  '{"description":"Add TOTP 2FA endpoints to the auth API","params":{"endpoints":"enable-2fa,verify-2fa,disable-2fa","library":"pquerna/otp"}}'
# Backend specialist implements and sends code back

# Step 3: Manager sends test task to QA specialist
pilotctl --json send-message 0:0000.0004.1A04 --wait 15m --data \
  '{"description":"Write and run tests for the 2FA API endpoints","params":{"coverage_target":"90"}}'
# QA specialist writes tests, runs them, returns results

# Step 4: Manager sends ML task (if 2FA includes risk scoring)
pilotctl --json send-message 0:0000.0004.1A03 --wait 30m --data \
  '{"description":"Train a login risk scoring model on auth logs","params":{"model_type":"gradient_boosting","features":"ip,device,time,location"}}'
# ML specialist trains model on GPU, sends model file back

# Step 5: Manager synthesizes all results
# Merges code from backend, test results from QA, model from ML
# Produces final PR with all components integrated

children.text: Each specialist executed on its own hardware, with its own credentials, in its own network position. The manager never needed GPU access, test database credentials, or CI configuration. It delegated the work and synthesized the results. This is the same pattern as local Claude agent teams, but distributed across the infrastructure that each task actually needs.
